name: Change Detection and Notification of Web Pages: A Survey. Mallawaarachchi, Meegahapola, Madhushanka, Heshan, Meedeniya and Jayarathna; ACM Computing Surveys vol. 53 no. 1, article 15, February 2020, 35 pages; preprint arXiv:1901.02660. The field it surveys is abbreviated CDN (Change Detection and Notification) -- unrelated to content delivery networks, and the collision is worth noting because it makes the literature hard to search. Predecessor surveys: Oita and Senellart's review of webpage change-detection approaches (source of the five-change-type taxonomy the survey adopts), and Shobhna and Chaudhary. Named systems and algorithms inside it: Mind-it (NetMind, 1996, the first CDN tool), ChangeDetection/Visualping, ChangeDetect, Google Alerts, Follow That Page, Wachete, WebVigil/CX-DIFF, the Delta framework (BULD Diff), X-Diff, Vi-DIFF, level-order traversal, Johnson's algorithm, the Proportional algorithm, shingling, cosine similarity, fuzzy tree difference, Bloom-filter URL/content hashing, and the Change Frequency Estimator Module (CFEM).
kind: Research result -- a survey paper. Secondarily a map of a class of commercial services (Visualping, Wachete, Google Alerts) and of a family of algorithms. Not a standard, not a benchmark, not a library.
maturity: The survey is published and stable (2020). The field it surveys is mature-to-stagnant: the foundational change-frequency studies are 2000-2012, the diff algorithms are 2000-2010 XML-era work, and the commercial services date from 1996-2010. Critically, the survey's frame is a POLLING, SERVER-SIDE, FETCH-AND-COMPARE world -- fetch a page periodically, store versions in a repository, diff the versions. Nothing in it addresses in-page observation of a live DOM, and the newest change-frequency figure it reports is from 2012. It should be read as a well-organised account of a pre-SPA problem, not as current practice.
license: The ACM Digital Library version is paywalled under ACM's terms; the arXiv preprint (1901.02660) and the author copy hosted at Old Dominion University are freely readable. Nothing is being adopted as code, so licence is irrelevant to use here; the ideas and figures are citable. Individual algorithms surveyed have their own licences and none is proposed for adoption.
keeps_and_discards: The CDN pipeline the survey describes keeps VERSIONS -- whole fetched pages saved into a version repository -- and derives change from comparing them. The survey notes these are typically stored unstructured, as tag-bearing documents, and that most change-detection mechanisms then convert a saved version into an XML-like tree where elements correspond to opening and closing HTML tags. So the retained artifact is the raw markup; the derived artifact is a diff. What the family discards varies by algorithm and is the survey's main axis: checksum and hash methods discard everything except a change/no-change bit; shingling and cosine methods discard structure and keep a similarity scalar; tree-diff methods (X-Diff, CX-DIFF, BULD Diff, Vi-DIFF, level-order traversal) keep structure and produce an edit script; signature methods (Johnson's, Proportional) discard everything except counts over declared signature categories -- paragraphs, headings, keywords, links -- which is a hand-declared feature vocabulary and is exactly the kind of pre-computed structural heuristic this project refuses. The survey also records a design goal that recurs throughout the field and matters here: distinguishing RELEVANT from IRRELEVANT change, with the Delta framework's explicit aim of ignoring advertisement churn. That is a semantic judgement about page regions and it is the field's dominant idea, which makes most of the field structure-dependent by design.
structure_preserved: The tree-diff branch preserves structure fully and is the only branch that does. The survey draws the ordered-versus-unordered tree distinction explicitly and it is the most transferable technical point in the paper: an ORDERED tree model treats left-to-right sibling order as significant, so any insertion shifts everything after it and registers as change; an UNORDERED model treats only ancestor relationships as significant, so a reordering is not a change. Level-order traversal (breadth-first over an ordered document tree) is the cheap ordered representative; X-Diff is the unordered representative and produces a minimum-cost edit script over an unordered tree using node signatures and an XHash. The survey reports the X-Diff authors' argument that the unordered model gives more accurate results. For this project the tension is direct: a positional-xpath key is an ORDERED model, and inherits exactly the fragility the ordered model has -- an insertion above a subtree renames everything below it. An unordered or signature-keyed model is what the survey's own preferred algorithm chose to avoid that. Shadow boundaries are entirely absent from the survey; the field predates shadow DOM and every representation is a single HTML document tree.
interactive_elements: Essentially unhandled, and the survey names this as a limitation of the field rather than solving it. The change-type taxonomy it adopts from Oita and Senellart includes BEHAVIOURAL changes -- defined as changes to active components such as embedded applications and scripts -- but the surveyed algorithms detect these only as changes to the script source text or to element attributes, never as changes to what a control does or what state it is in. Commercial CDN services monitor 'text, images, links, documents (PDF, DOC, DOCX)' per the survey's own list of monitoring options, with no control or state category at all. A page whose controls change state without changing markup is invisible to every system surveyed.
interactive_state_fidelity: Zero across the field, and the reason is structural: these systems compare FETCHED markup, so they see only server-declared initial state. Attribute-reflected state (disabled, checked as an attribute, aria-*) would in principle be caught by the tree-diff and attribute-change branches -- the taxonomy's ATTRIBUTE (presentation) change category covers attribute edits -- but a fetch-based system never sees user-driven or script-driven state at all, because it never runs the page. The taxonomy is nonetheless a useful vocabulary to reuse: content / structural (layout) / attribute (presentation) / behavioural / type change is a clean five-way partition of what can change in a document, and TYPE change (a p tag becoming a div) is a category most delta schemes forget and which matters here because it changes the tag component of an address without changing content or position.
layout_awareness: Mostly none, with one explicit exception. The bulk of the surveyed algorithms operate on markup and text only. Vi-DIFF is the exception and is described as detecting content and structural changes INCLUDING the visual representation of webpages, and as being able to detect semantic differences between two versions -- it segments the rendered page visually before diffing. The survey records its cost honestly: Vi-DIFF may cost more resources and time than other methods, and it groups Vi-DIFF with CX-DIFF as computationally expensive enough to risk overloading servers. The taxonomy's ATTRIBUTE (presentation) change category -- fonts, colours, captions -- is a layout-adjacent notion detected through markup rather than through geometry. For this project the reading is: the one visual method in the survey is also the most expensive, and it lives on the far side of the no-layout-in-the-fold line.
javascript_required: No, and this is the field's largest blind spot relative to the modern web. The surveyed architecture is a crawler that fetches a URL and stores the response; scripts do not run. The survey's own dynamism figures are therefore measured over server-delivered markup, which means every reported change rate is a rate of CHANGE IN DELIVERED HTML and not a rate of change in what a user sees. On a client-rendered page the delivered HTML can be byte-identical across months while the rendered content changes hourly, so the widely quoted 'about 65% of pages had zero change' figure systematically UNDERSTATES change for any page whose content is assembled in the browser. This is the single most important reach caveat on every number in the paper and it should be stated whenever they are quoted.
evaluation_method: As a survey, its method is classification and comparison rather than measurement: it partitions CDN systems by architecture (server-side versus client-side), by scheduling and change-frequency estimation approach, by change-detection algorithm, and by notification and visualisation mechanism, then tabulates methodology, advantages, disadvantages and source work per algorithm. The comparison tables are qualitative -- advantage and disadvantage prose, not numbers -- which is the survey's principal weakness: it summarises what each algorithm's authors claimed about it rather than running any of them against a common corpus. The genuinely empirical material it collects is the set of longitudinal change-frequency studies it tabulates, whose method is uniform and imitable: crawl a fixed URL set on a fixed schedule, hash or diff successive versions, report the distribution of change. Cho and Garcia-Molina used MD5 checksum equality as the change criterion, which is the crudest possible oracle and counts a whitespace edit as a change, so the reported rates are upper bounds on change and lower bounds on stability.
corpus_size_and_origins: The survey itself has no corpus. The corpora of the studies it tabulates, with their reach, are: Cho and Garcia-Molina 2000 -- 720,000 webpages from 270 WEBSITES, crawled daily for 4 months, so origin diversity is only 270 despite the page count, and the sites were selected from a US-centric 1999-2000 web; Fetterly et al. 2003 -- approximately 150 million pages over 11 weeks, by far the largest and the only one with real origin breadth, but restricted to whatever a 2002-era crawler could fetch; Adar et al. 2009 -- approximately 55,000 pages, selected because USERS REVISITED them, which is a strong and useful selection bias (it measures the pages people actually watch, not the web) ; Elsas and Dumais 2010 -- approximately 2,000,000 HTML pages crawled weekly for 10 weeks; Saad and Gancarski 2012 -- just over 100 pages from the France Televisions archive, crawled hourly yielding over 3,000 versions per day, so it is deep-in-time and near-zero in breadth, and it is the only non-English-web corpus in the set. Aggregate reach: the newest is 2012, all predate the single-page-application era, all are fetch-based, and all except Fetterly are narrow in origin count. These are exactly the CleanEval-style reach limits the fields file exists to force into the open -- large page counts concealing small origin counts and a fourteen-year-old newest observation.
reported_precision_recall: No precision/recall figures for any detection algorithm appear in the survey; the algorithm comparison is qualitative throughout, which is a real and citable gap. The quantitative content is change-rate distributions, reported here with their denominators. Cho and Garcia-Molina 2000, denominator 720,000 pages from 270 sites over 4 months of daily crawls with MD5 as the change test: more than 20% of pages showed a change on EVERY visit; 40% of pages changed within a week; over 50% of .com and .edu pages did not change at all across the whole 4 months. Fetterly et al. 2003, denominator ~150 million pages over 11 weeks: approximately 65% showed zero change over the period; .org and .gov changed less than .edu; spam-bearing pages changed more frequently. Adar et al. 2009, denominator ~55,000 user-revisited pages: 34% showed no change; the remainder showed at least one change every 123 hours; popular pages changed more than unpopular ones; sports, news and personal pages changed most; .gov and .edu least. Elsas and Dumais 2010, denominator ~2,000,000 pages over 10 weekly crawls: over 62% showed no virtual difference; highly relevant documents were both more likely to change and changed by larger amounts. Saad and Gancarski 2012, denominator ~100 FranceTV pages crawled hourly: root-level pages such as homepages changed significantly, deep pages did not. Two cross-cutting readings matter for this project: change is heavily concentrated -- a minority of pages account for nearly all of it -- and change rate is strongly predicted by DEPTH within a site, with homepages and index pages volatile and leaf pages stable. Both argue for per-URL adaptive scheduling rather than uniform recrawl.
independent_oracle: Weak throughout. The change-frequency studies use checksum equality, which is a self-consistent test with no external reference: a page that serves a rotating timestamp or a random advertisement registers as changed on every fetch and there is no oracle distinguishing that from a real edit. The survey acknowledges the problem indirectly by devoting space to relevant-versus-irrelevant change and to the Delta framework's ad-ignoring goal, which is an admission that the naive oracle over-reports. No study in the set uses human judgement of whether a change mattered, and no algorithm is validated against a human-labelled change corpus. Note also the Fetterly figure -- 65% zero change -- and the Cho figure -- over 50% of .com and .edu unchanged in 4 months -- are the same claim measured differently and they are broadly consistent, which is the only cross-study agreement available and is weak evidence of the checksum oracle's stability rather than of its correctness.
evidence_independence: Mixed but better than the tool-comparison items in this set. The survey is written by academics with no product in the field, so its classification is independent of the systems it describes -- but it reports each algorithm's advantages and disadvantages from the algorithm's OWN authors' papers, so the per-algorithm claims are author-run and are being relayed rather than verified. The change-frequency studies are independent academic measurements of third-party websites, which is genuine independence. The commercial CDN services (Visualping, Wachete, Google Alerts, Follow That Page) are described from their public documentation with no measurement of any kind, so no vendor performance claim in this area is corroborated anywhere. Bottom line: the change-rate numbers are independent and citable with their reach caveats; every algorithm-quality statement traces to that algorithm's authors and must not be presented as a comparison.
page_archetype_coverage: This is one of the survey's stronger contributions, because the change-rate studies break down by page type and the breakdown is consistent across four independent studies. News, sports and personal pages change most; government and educational domains change least; .org and .gov are the most stable top-level domains and .edu less so; spam-bearing pages churn heavily; homepages and archive-root pages change far more than deep leaf pages; and the pages users actually revisit (Adar's selection) change more than the web at large. Translated into this project's archetypes: listing, feed and collection pages are the volatile class, article and documentation pages are the stable class, and service or transactional pages are absent from these studies entirely because a fetch-based crawler cannot reach them. Any single aggregate change rate mixes a near-100%-daily population with a near-0% population, and the survey's own tables make that mixing visible, which is more than most of the extraction literature does.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Barely addressed. Four of the five change-rate studies are on the anglophone web; only Saad and Gancarski's ~100 FranceTV pages are non-English, and French is Latin-script. No CJK, RTL or whitespace-free-segmentation evidence appears anywhere in the survey. The algorithmic implications are real and unexamined: shingling and cosine methods tokenise on whitespace and therefore behave differently on Chinese, Japanese and Thai text; the survey notes as a shingling limitation only that very small content cannot generate sufficient shingles, which is the Latin-script version of a problem that is far worse in scripts where the tokeniser is wrong to begin with. Hash and tree-diff methods are script-invariant. Unicode normalisation is not mentioned anywhere, and for a checksum-based change oracle a normalisation change on the server registers as a total page change, which is a plausible and unmeasured source of false change in these very studies.
leaks_outward: Substantial for the architecture the survey describes, and this is a real contrast with the project's in-page approach. A server-side CDN service fetches the monitored page on a schedule from its own infrastructure, so the target origin sees repeated automated requests with a recognisable cadence and a service-identifying user agent; the origin learns which of its pages someone is watching and how often. The USER, meanwhile, discloses to the CDN service the full list of URLs they care about, the page regions they selected for monitoring, and by implication their interests -- which for a third-party hosted service is a significant disclosure. The client-side architecture the survey contrasts it with moves the polling to the user's own machine, which removes the third-party disclosure but makes the request pattern attributable to the user's own IP. The project's in-page sensor has neither problem for pages the operator is already visiting, and inherits the second one for any page it fetches on its own.
mechanism_detectability: High for the surveyed systems and this is worth stating because it is the axis on which polling loses to observation. A polling CDN is trivially detectable server-side: fixed-interval requests to the same URL from the same address with no referrer and no asset fetches is one of the most recognisable crawler signatures there is, and the survey itself notes that many crawlers do not honour robots.txt and that sites impose request-frequency and data-allowance limits in response. Adaptive scheduling driven by estimated change frequency makes the pattern LESS regular and therefore slightly less detectable, which is an unremarked side benefit of the Poisson-estimator work. An in-page MutationObserver is not detectable in this way at all -- it makes no requests -- which is a decisive architectural argument for observation over polling wherever the page is one the operator is genuinely visiting.
countermeasures: Against the target site's defences the survey offers only compliance: honour robots.txt, respect crawl-delay and data allowances, and reduce request volume by estimating change frequency so that fetches that would find nothing are not made. Change-frequency estimation is in fact the field's main efficiency and politeness mechanism, and the survey frames it exactly that way -- reduce the number of page checks where no change is detected. Against false change (advertisement rotation, timestamps, session tokens), the countermeasures are the relevance-filtering approaches: the Delta framework's DOM normalisation and change clustering, region-scoped monitoring (Jain and Khandagale's zone changes, and the commercial services' select-a-region feature), and thresholding on percentage change. Every one of these is a structural heuristic and every one is therefore off-limits to this project as specified.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured. The field's central tradeoff -- filtering irrelevant change costs you some relevant change -- is asserted everywhere in the survey and quantified nowhere. No study reports how many real changes a relevance filter or a change threshold suppresses, against a control of unfiltered diffing. Similarly, the cost of adaptive scheduling is stated qualitatively (you will miss changes on pages you check too rarely) and never given as a measured miss rate against a control of continuous polling, even though Saad and Gancarski's hourly FranceTV crawl -- 3,000+ versions daily over ~100 pages -- is exactly the dense ground truth against which a sparser schedule's miss rate could have been computed. That experiment is available and unpublished. [uncertain] -- absence of measurement asserted from the survey's own tables being qualitative; a specific paper may report such a figure without the survey relaying it.
gate_state_at_capture: Not addressed anywhere. The surveyed systems fetch anonymously, so their captures are by construction of the ungated public representation, and pages behind consent, paywall or login are simply monitored in whatever state an anonymous fetch returns -- which for a paywalled page means the CDN system faithfully monitors the paywall interstitial and reports it as stable. No study reports what fraction of its corpus was in that condition, so the reported change rates are silently mixed over gated and ungated captures. Given that consent interfaces became near-ubiquitous after these studies were run, this is a further reason not to transfer the numbers forward: a modern rerun would be measuring banners as much as content.
determinism: Per algorithm: hash and checksum comparison is fully deterministic; ordered tree-diff and level-order traversal are deterministic; unordered tree matching (X-Diff) is deterministic given a fixed node-signature and hashing scheme but its result depends on that scheme, and unordered tree edit distance is in general a much harder problem than the ordered case, so implementations restrict it and different restrictions give different edit scripts for the same input pair; shingling and cosine methods are deterministic given a fixed tokeniser and shingle width, and silently different across tokenisers; the fuzzy tree-difference method requires, in the survey's own words, defining a suitable fuzzy hash function, so its output is a function of an undisclosed parameter choice -- the same pattern as the fuzzy re-anchoring problem in item 23, and the same conclusion applies: undisclosed thresholds make a result non-reproducible from its description. Systemically, the whole pipeline is non-deterministic upstream of the algorithm because the page fetched at time t is not the page fetched at time t+1 for reasons unrelated to editing.
determinism_across_versions: For fetch-based systems there is no browser and therefore no browser-version drift -- an unexpected advantage of the old architecture. The drift that does occur is in the HTML parser used to build the comparison tree: two parsers disagree about implied elements, whitespace nodes and error recovery, so the same version pair diffs differently under different parsers, and the survey does not mention parsing at all. For the project, the transferable warning is that the tree you diff must be produced by a pinned parser, and a parser change is a corpus-wide re-baselining event.
reproducibility: Very low for the empirical results and the survey does not conceal it: every change-rate study measured the live web at a specific past time, none preserved the fetched versions as a public artifact, and the URL sets are not published in reusable form. None of the five studies can be re-run. This is the same defect the project has in its own corpus (75% of pages fetching live resources on every read) and the field's history shows what it costs: a set of numbers that have been quoted for two decades and cannot be checked, updated or disaggregated by anyone. The corrective, and it is the field's clearest lesson for this project, is that a change-detection result is only reproducible if the VERSIONS are kept, not just the diffs -- which is what the CDN architecture's version repository does and what a pure delta stream does not.
failure_modes: The survey catalogues these per algorithm and the list generalises well. (1) False change from irrelevant churn: advertisements, timestamps, rotating banners, session identifiers, and view counters make checksum and naive diff methods report change on every fetch -- this is the field's dominant failure and the reason the Delta framework exists. (2) Missed change from coarse scheduling: a page that changes and reverts between two polls is invisible, and polling can never see intermediate states, which is a structural limitation of the whole architecture and one that in-page observation does not share. (3) Cost blowup on large trees: the survey notes CX-DIFF and Vi-DIFF are computationally expensive enough to risk overloading servers, that the BULD Diff's performance degrades proportionally to tree depth, and that the tree-comparison work of Jain and Khandagale does not specify a depth limit, which is inefficient on large trees. (4) Insufficient signal on small content: shingling cannot generate enough shingles from very small documents. (5) Category blindness per algorithm: Johnson's algorithm does not detect changes to links; level-order traversal detects that a change occurred at a tree level without giving enough information about what it was. (6) Unordered-versus-ordered mismatch: an ordered model reports a reordering as a large change, an unordered model reports a genuine reordering as no change -- there is no setting that is right for both, and the choice must match what the consumer cares about. (7) Threshold misconfiguration: percentage-of-change thresholds are user-set and silently suppress everything below them.
failure_visibility: Silent in almost every case, and in the same direction as the rest of this research set. A missed change produces no notification, which is indistinguishable from no change having occurred -- the user cannot tell a working monitor from a broken one, and the survey does not discuss any liveness or self-test mechanism for CDN systems. A false change produces a spurious notification, which at least is visible, and the field's whole relevance-filtering effort is aimed at that visible failure while the invisible one goes unaddressed. This asymmetry is instructive: the field optimised hard against the failure users complain about and not at all against the failure users cannot see. The project should not repeat that; the analogue here is that blind spots in the delta channel (item 24) are the invisible failure and must be tested for deliberately.
scale_limits: Two distinct walls. On the DIFF side, tree-edit-distance methods are the expensive class: ordered tree edit distance is polynomial but with a bad exponent for large trees, unordered tree edit distance is intractable in general and X-Diff's practicality comes from restricting it with node signatures and XHash; the survey's own summary flags CX-DIFF and Vi-DIFF as capable of overloading servers and BULD Diff as degrading with tree depth. So diff cost is superlinear in DOM size, which is why the field's cheap methods (checksums, level-order traversal, signature counts) are the ones actually deployed. On the FETCH side, cost is linear in monitored pages times poll frequency, and the entire change-frequency-estimation literature exists to reduce the second factor -- the Poisson framing, Cho and Garcia-Molina's estimators, the staleness metric and optimal-refresh formulation, and CFEM's two-phase approach of crawling a fresh page to learn its rate then scheduling to it. What the survey does NOT discuss, at all, is the cost of the VERSION REPOSITORY as it grows -- storing every version of every monitored page is the field's largest data cost, and there is no analysis of retrieval or write cost as the repository scales. That silence is directly relevant below.
delta_cost_model: The field has no per-change cost model in the project's sense, and its architecture is the opposite of one: cost is per POLL, not per change, and the entire point of change-frequency estimation is to reduce the number of polls that find nothing. A poll costs a full fetch plus a full diff regardless of whether anything changed, so the cost is proportional to the PAGE and to the schedule, never to the delta. This is worth stating plainly because it is the clearest available contrast with an observation-based design: polling is O(page) per check, observation is O(mutation) per change, and the survey's whole scheduling literature is an elaborate way to make an O(page) operation affordable rather than a way to make it O(delta). Named exclusions if one tried to read a delta model out of the field anyway: the fetch itself is unavoidable and unbounded by the change; the tree construction is O(page); the diff is superlinear in page for the tree-based methods; changes that occur and revert between polls cost nothing and are also never seen, so the model trades cost against completeness in a way no in-page observer has to; and the version repository grows by a full page per poll unless deduplicated, which the survey does not discuss.
reanchoring_stability: Addressed only implicitly, through the ordered-versus-unordered tree distinction and through region-scoped monitoring. Jain and Khandagale's zone-change work is the closest thing to re-anchoring in the survey: the user selects a region of a page and the system localises detection to that node and its children -- which requires the selected node to be re-findable across versions, and the survey does not say how it is re-found or what happens when it is not. That silence is the field's largest unexamined assumption, and it is the same assumption item 23 measured and found to fail 22-27% of the time. X-Diff's node signatures and XHash are the closest mechanism to a content-hash re-anchor in the survey and are worth noting as a 2003-vintage precedent for hashing a node's structural and content identity to match it across versions rather than addressing it positionally. No re-anchor rate is reported anywhere in the survey.
adversarial_exposure: The survey's only adversarial observation is empirical rather than defensive: Fetterly et al. found that spam-bearing pages change more frequently than others, so change rate itself is weakly discriminative of adversarial content. Otherwise the field assumes a cooperative page. The exposures it does not consider and which transfer directly: a page can DEFEAT change detection by churning irrelevant content to bury a real edit in noise, and can defeat it more cheaply by making its markup change on every fetch so that checksum-based detection saturates -- both are trivially available and the field's whole relevance-filtering effort is an unwitting arms race against them. A page can also EXPLOIT change detection by making a monitored region change in a way that triggers a notification the user acts on. And because these systems preserve whatever markup is fetched, they preserve invisible content on equal terms with visible content, with no more ability to filter concealment than any other layout-blind fetch-based approach.
provenance_carrying: Weak. The stored artifact is a version of a page keyed by URL and fetch time, which gives origin and capture time but no intra-page address -- change is reported as a diff between documents, not as a change at an address. The tree-diff branch does produce node-level results and therefore could carry per-node provenance, but the survey does not discuss recording it and the notification layer flattens everything to human-readable added/removed text (the near-universal green-added, red-struck-deleted rendering it describes). Shadow depth and gate state are absent as concepts. Relative to the project's trie key, the field's provenance is a strict subset -- URL and time only -- which is another way of saying the project's address-as-provenance property is not something this literature supplies.
roundtrip_safety: Not treated. The relevant round trip in this field would be: given version A and a computed edit script, apply the script to A and check the result equals version B. That is a free, oracle-independent correctness test for any diff algorithm, it is the exact analogue of the serialise-parse-serialise fixed point, and the survey reports no algorithm being validated this way. Given that the field's algorithm comparisons are entirely qualitative, applying this one test to the surveyed algorithms would have produced more information than the whole comparison table. It should be a standing test on any diff the project computes.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not an LLM-era literature and it emits no tokens, but the notification layer is a budgeted-summary problem in disguise and has one transferable idea: users are shown a THRESHOLDED, RELEVANCE-FILTERED, VISUALLY-DIFFED summary rather than a full page, because the whole point is to not re-read the page. The green-added/red-deleted convention and the percentage-of-change threshold are a decades-old answer to 'what do you show someone who already knows the old state', which is exactly the question a change-driven emission to a model has to answer. The ordering implication is that a change summary should lead with WHAT CHANGED and reference the unchanged context by address rather than restating it -- and given that position bias becomes recency-dominant past roughly half the context fill, placing the change last rather than first is the right call for a model, which is the opposite of what a human-facing notification does. Worth an explicit design decision rather than an inherited convention.
representation_cost: Storage cost in this architecture is a full page version per poll, which is the dominant and undiscussed cost; the survey mentions Bloom filters for duplicate URL and content detection as the field's one storage economy, and does not analyse repository growth. Diff computation cost is superlinear in DOM size for the tree methods and linear for the cheap ones. In token terms: nothing, since the output is a human-facing diff. The relevant lesson is negative -- the field kept every version and never analysed what that cost, which is precisely the kind of silent store-growth problem the project has measured and which this literature therefore cannot help with.
what_could_be_adopted: Four things, and one important non-answer. (1) THE FIVE-WAY CHANGE TAXONOMY (content / structural-layout / attribute-presentation / behavioural / type), from Oita and Senellart via this survey. It is a clean, structure-agnostic partition -- it classifies WHAT KIND of change occurred without naming what the region means -- and TYPE change in particular (a p becoming a div) is a category most delta designs forget and which specifically breaks tag-component addressing. Adopting it as the vocabulary for classifying mutation records costs nothing and makes the delta stream self-describing. (2) THE ORDERED-VERSUS-UNORDERED TREE DISTINCTION as an explicit design decision rather than an accident. The project's positional-xpath key silently commits to the ordered model and therefore to its fragility; X-Diff's authors argued the unordered model is more accurate, and the node-signature/XHash mechanism they used to make unordered matching tractable is the 2003 ancestor of the content-hash re-anchoring recommended in item 23. (3) CHANGE-FREQUENCY ESTIMATION PER URL, in the Poisson-process form (Cho and Garcia-Molina's estimators, the staleness metric, CFEM's learn-then-schedule loop), for deciding recapture cadence -- directly applicable to scheduling the periodic full-recapture oracle item 24 requires, since that oracle's cost should be spent where change is likely rather than uniformly. The empirical priors are usable too: change concentrates in a minority of pages, correlates with popularity and with shallow depth in a site, and is near-zero for documentation and government content. (4) THE APPLY-THE-DIFF ROUND-TRIP TEST described above, which the field never ran and which is free. THE NON-ANSWER, stated explicitly because it was the reason to research this item: THIS LITERATURE DOES NOT KNOW THE INGEST-DEGRADATION FAILURE MODE. The survey has no analysis of version-repository growth, no per-write cost model, and no measurement of storage-side degradation of any kind; its entire cost discussion is about FETCH volume and DIFF computation. There is no standard remedy here for a store whose write cost triples as it grows, because the field never measured the store. That question belongs to the dedup-storage and LSM/B-tree literature covered under item 22 -- disk-bottleneck index lookups, write amplification with tree depth, and allocator/GC pressure proportional to live object count -- and the honest finding is that the change-detection literature is the wrong place to look for it.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: MIXED, LEANING REJECTED. The field's dominant idea -- distinguishing relevant from irrelevant change, exemplified by the Delta framework's goal of ignoring advertisement churn and by the commercial services' select-a-region monitoring -- is precisely a pre-computed structural heuristic naming page regions, and is REJECTED. Signature-based methods (Johnson's, Proportional) that count changes over declared categories of paragraphs, headings, keywords and links are a hand-built feature vocabulary and are REJECTED. The five-way change taxonomy and the ordered/unordered tree distinction are purely structural descriptions with no semantic naming and are ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Checksum, shingling and tree-diff mechanics are content-agnostic and ADOPTABLE AS-IS. no_layout_in_the_fold: Vi-DIFF, the one visual-segmentation method, is ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY, and the survey's own note that it is among the most expensive methods reinforces keeping it off the hot path. Everything else in the survey is markup-only and ADOPTABLE AS-IS. o_delta: REJECTED AS AN ARCHITECTURE, ADOPTABLE AS A SCHEDULER. Poll-and-diff is O(page) per check by construction and is the antithesis of incremental observation; nothing in the architecture should be adopted. The change-frequency estimation layer, however, is ADOPTABLE AS-IS for deciding when to pay the O(page) verification cost that item 24's soundness oracle requires. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS with a caveat -- the field's studies are all real-web measurements, but their reproducibility failure (no preserved versions, no published URL sets, newest data from 2012) means their FIGURES function as NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY: quotable as historical evidence that change is concentrated and archetype-dependent, not usable as current rates, and definitely not usable for a client-rendered web the fetch-based method could not see. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO INTERACTION; the field predates shadow DOM entirely and offers neither a temptation nor a technique. OVERALL VERDICT: the taxonomy and the scheduling mathematics are adoptable as-is; the relevance-filtering and region-selection core of the field is rejected on structure_agnosticism; the poll-and-diff architecture is rejected on o_delta; and the empirical figures are negative-oracle-only because of their age, their fetch-based blindness to client rendering, and their unreproducibility.
governance_signal_handling: The survey addresses robots.txt directly and its observation is the field's most honest: robots.txt had been adopted by over 30% of webpages by 2007, and many web crawlers do not abide by it. It lists the constraints sites impose -- restricting structural changes, limiting request frequency, and capping downloadable data allowances -- as things a well-behaved CDN crawler must respect, and frames change-frequency estimation partly as a politeness mechanism that reduces useless fetches. Nothing newer appears: Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth and HTTP 402 all postdate the survey and none is discussed. The transferable point is architectural rather than normative -- a polling monitor is a crawler and is subject to crawler governance, whereas an in-page observer on a page the operator is already viewing is not making requests at all, so the two architectures sit on opposite sides of every one of these mechanisms. That distinction should be recorded explicitly rather than assumed.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The survey has no privacy or legal discussion whatsoever, which is itself notable for a field whose systems retain full copies of third-party web pages indefinitely in version repositories. The exposures implied by the architecture: a hosted CDN service holds a persistent, timestamped archive of arbitrary third-party pages including any personal data on them, plus a per-user record of which URLs and which page regions each subscriber cares about -- the latter being behavioural profiling data of some sensitivity. Under a regime treating persistent retention of page content as the regulated act, a version repository is squarely in scope and the survey offers no retention, minimisation or erasure discussion at all. For this project the transferable design point is that keeping versions is what makes change detection reproducible (see reproducibility) and simultaneously what makes it a data-protection liability, so the retention decision should be explicit, per-origin, prefix-scoped for erasure, and bounded rather than indefinite. [uncertain] on any specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
